The archive

A few things saved from the years at Warner Bros., and the stories behind them.

03 / The Warner Bros. years

The office that felt bigger than life.

I loved visiting Dad at work. Mostly because of the walls.

From Ashley's memories

The walls were covered.

Dad worked in promotion, so his office at Warner Bros. was covered with posters and promotional material for whatever records were coming out next. (check out that James Taylor Walking Man poster behind him in this pic!) I loved going there. It always felt a little bigger than life, and I could spend forever staring at everything around me.

Some of those posters ended up at home, too. Dad used them to cover the drywall in his studio.

I love this picture of Mom and Dad in his office.

From the file cabinet · Record World · September 18, 1976 · p. 6

A thank-you from Fleetwood Mac.

In this 1976 Record World feature, Fleetwood Mac thanked the Warner Bros. promotion team with personally signed album-cover enlargements. Dad is pictured in the front row, holding one of them. We still have that signed piece in the family.

05 / Objects with stories

Not just souvenirs.

Two things that used to hang in our house. Neither is there now.

Travis Tritt · A Christmas gift

Travis wearing the suit. Photo from Dad’s collection.

Travis's missing leather suit.

For years, the Manuel of Hollywood suit Travis wore on the cover of T-R-O-U-B-L-E hung in a glass case on our studio wall. He'd given it to Dad for Christmas.

Dad later lent it to Atlanta's Hard Rock Cafe. Someone smashed the display case and stole the suit. After the restaurant settled with Dad, he used the money to buy Travis a home recording studio for Christmas the following year. Dad turned the whole mess into another gift for Travis.

Read the newspaper clipping · December 1, 1993 · p. E2 ↗

The Warner Bros. guitar · Mossman Superlative

The Mossman guitar, photographed for Dad’s book.

The Bugs Bunny guitar.

Dad had Scott Baxendale build him a custom Mossman Superlative with Warner Bros. and Looney Tunes inlays. Travis played it in the “Country Club” video. At our house, it had its own temperature-controlled case.

Dad later sold much of his collection. In his book, he says Baxendale told him the guitar had made its way to a museum in California. A guitar dealer in Tokyo now has it listed for ¥6.6 million (including tax), roughly $41,700 USD at the October 9, 2026 exchange rate. See the guitar and its listing ↗

How Scott and Dad designed and built the guitar, with photos ↗

06 / The file cabinet

The stories have receipts.

Old trade publications, personnel announcements and a few things worth keeping.

Billboard · October 4, 1975 · p. 8

A name in the trade papers

Growing up, I knew Dad worked in the music business. I just didn’t fully appreciate how strange it was that my own father occasionally appeared in Billboard magazine.

He never talked about these features, and I actually didn’t know they existed until I was doing some research for the show. SO. WEIRD.

Examine the clipping ↗
Gibson Guitars · The Birth of the Les Paul · p. 188

One for the guitar books. (Literally).

Dad’s name turns up somewhere else, too: beside a photograph of a 1956 Les Paul in Gibson Guitars: 100 Years of an American Icon by Walter Carter. The feature, “The Birth of the Les Paul,” is by Tom Wheeler.

See the feature and book cover · p. 188 ↗
Billboard · January 24, 1976 · p. 4

Atlanta was just the beginning.

In January 1976, Billboard reported that Dad had moved from local promotion in Atlanta to Warner Bros.’ regional marketing manager for the South. His work had grown from one city to a whole region, helping connect the label’s artists with radio stations, record stores, and the people who would become their biggest fans.

Examine the clipping ↗
Billboard · September 27, 1986 · p. 50

An award worth keeping

Another clipping from the collection, this time naming Dad among Warner Bros. promotion award recipients.

Examine the clipping ↗
From Dad’s saved letters

The men who believed in Dad.

Before Dad could become someone who opened doors for other artists, there were people who opened doors for him.

Two of those people were Mo Ostin, chairman of Warner Bros. Records, and Joe Smith, the label’s president. Mo brought Jimi Hendrix to Reprise, and Joe signed the Grateful Dead to Warner Bros., which is a fairly ridiculous amount of American music history to fit into one sentence. Their willingness to recognize something special and give it room to grow helped shape the music so many of us grew up loving.

Dad respected them enormously, and he personally admired the men behind those titles. They believed in his instincts and his ability, and their confidence helped him believe in himself.

In January 1975, Mo wrote to congratulate Dad on being Warner’s Promotion Man of the Year for 1974, thanking him for his dedication and commitment. Joe sent congratulations, too, although his letter included enough affectionate ribbing to suggest that winning an award would earn Dad absolutely no protection from being heckled by the president of the company.

Dad saved both letters.

Years later, after Joe died, his son Jeff personally invited Mom and Dad to the memorial in Beverly Hills. They couldn’t attend, but Jeff shared details afterward, including recorded tributes from James Taylor, Garth Brooks, and the Eagles. James spoke about Joe and played a few bars of “Fire and Rain,” which seems like a pretty extraordinary way to be remembered.

What moved Dad was the love running through all of it. These were people whose music had shaped generations, remembering someone who had believed in them. Dad understood that feeling. He had been on the receiving end of Joe’s encouragement, too.

When I look at these letters now, I understand why Dad kept them. Imagine spending your life loving music, then discovering that the people helping shape its future believed you belonged there, too.

From our family collection

A house full of music.

Guitars and instruments were part of the furniture in our house (literally, in this photo). Dad collected them, played them, and found room for them everywhere.

When I think about home, I hear those instruments as much as I picture the rooms they were in. They were such a big part of Dad’s life that they became part of mine, too. Long before I had a playlist of my own, I was growing up inside his.
